DefaultBatcher, L65 declares vertexSize = 6 at L81: for each vertex, two floats of screen-space position, two floats of UV, one packed uint32 ARGB color, and one packed uint32 holding the texture slot id and the round-pixels flag. packQuadAttributes, L152 transforms the four corners with the sprite’s world matrix (a 2×2 plus translation — pure arithmetic on a Float32Array) and writes the textureIdAndRound word as (textureId << 16) | roundPixels.

The batch pipe (BatcherPipe, L29) owns one active batcher at a time. addToBatch at L91 breaks the batch when the element’s batcher name differs — custom geometry goes through a different batcher — and batchers are created with maxTextures taken from renderer.limits.maxBatchableTextures. Where does that number come from? On WebGL, getMaxTexturesPerBatch, L14 probes MAX_TEXTURE_IMAGE_UNITS and then binary-searches how many if-statements the fragment shader can actually carry; on WebGPU, GpuLimitsSystem, L55 takes min(maxSampledTexturesPerShaderStage, maxSamplersPerShaderStage) straight from the device.

When a batch must split — different blend mode, different topology, or no free texture slot — Batcher.break, L484 flushes the accumulated range as a Batch instruction (pooled objects, so breaking is allocation-free at steady state) and starts the next one. At the end of the walk, buildEnd, L117 points the shared BatchGeometry buffers at the batch data, upload, L134 marks only dirty buffer ranges, and execute, L152 delegates to the backend adaptor. One drawElements call per batch; thousands of sprites per call.

One Scene Graph, Two GPU Backends

Because batching produces plain buffers and instruction objects, the backend is just an execution strategy. Both WebGLRenderer, L163 and WebGPURenderer, L158 extend AbstractRenderer, L204, whose render at L345 forces the stage into a render group and fires the prerender/renderStart/render/renderEnd/postrender runners. Runners (SystemRunner, L44) call same-named methods on every registered system, so a renderer is assembled from dozens of small systems — view, background, state, texture, geometry, batch — each tagged with the backends it supports.

Backend-specific work is isolated in adaptors: the batch pipe talks to GlBatchAdaptor or GpuBatchAdaptor, and WebGPU-only concepts live in the gpu/ tree — GpuDeviceSystem owns the device, BindGroupSystem caches bind groups for texture batches, and a PSO cache keys compiled shader-state objects so identical sprites reuse them. Shared services stay backend-neutral: TexturePool, L75 recycles render textures by size bucket through getOptimalTexture, L211, and global uniforms upload the world matrix once per frame. If you know three-js, the split feels familiar — there too, one scene graph feeds multiple renderer backends — and the same “many objects, few draw calls” math is why Phaser-class 2D game frameworks build their rendering on top of this kind of batcher.

Honest Limits

  • WebGL is still the default, not WebGPU. The code says so itself: autoDetectRenderer’s doc comment at L47 explains WebGL is prioritized “as it is the most tested safe API,” with WebGPU to be prioritized “in the near future.” You must pass preference: 'webgpu' (verified against isWebGPUSupported) to opt in.
  • A bad preference array can throw. If you restrict preference to backends the browser cannot provide, autoDetectRenderer raises No available renderer for the current environment at L167 — there is no silent last-resort beyond your list.
  • Batches are not free. Every blend-mode change, topology change, or texture-slot overflow splits the batch into another draw call. Heavy scenes mixing many blend modes and textures still pay per-batch overhead; the batcher’s own comment calls this out at L479.
  • v8 is a breaking change from v7. Custom shaders migrate through a helper (migrateFragmentFromV7toV8.ts exists for GL fragment code), and long-lived APIs are deprecated in-tree: Container.mixin since 8.8.0, TexturePool.textureStyle since 8.21.0, and the second argument of renderer.render since 8.0.0. Upgrading means reading the deprecation notes, not just the changelog.
  • The batcher contract tightened. Since v8.8.0, constructing a Batcher without an explicit maxTextures triggers a deprecation warning at L397 — batch capacity is now per-renderer configuration, not a global guess.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of PixiJS v8: how the Ticker, scene graph, render pipes, and sprite batcher turn thousands of sprites into a handful of draw calls on WebGL and WebGPU.

entry.title: Inside raylib: How the Minimal C Game Library Draws a Frame

link.title: Inside raylib: How the Minimal C Game Library Draws a Frame

entry.content:
Every newcomer hits the same wall with a full engine: to draw one red circle you inherit a scene tree, an asset importer, an editor layout, and a build system you did not choose. Engines like Godot earn that complexity for large teams, but for a first window, a first sprite, or a lecture demo, the price of admission is simply too high. raylib’s answer is almost aggressive: a handful of C files, one public header, no editor, no scene graph — you can genuinely read the whole thing in a weekend. The obvious question is how a library that fits in your head still talks to a GPU driver, a window manager, and an audio device at the same time.

The two lines every raylib program shares are BeginDrawing() and EndDrawing(). They look like decorative sugar, something you could skip. They are not. Everything between them is recorded into CPU-side buffers, and the second call is where the GPU actually gets fed, where the swap happens, where the frame rate is enforced, and where input events are polled for the next frame. Understanding those two functions is understanding how raylib thinks.

And then there is the portability trick. The same rcore.c that opens a GLFW window on Windows also drives Android, a bare Linux framebuffer via DRM/KMS, and a browser canvas under Emscripten. One file, no #ifdef spaghetti in your application code, because the platform-specific half was split into ten small files behind a fixed contract. This post walks that whole path — from your call to DrawCircleV() down to the raw glDrawElements — using only the actual sources on master.

raylib's module layering: rcore owns the window and the frame bracket, per-platform files own the OS, rlgl owns OpenGL, and the four drawing modules plus raudio sit on top as thin, optional layers.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything the application sees is one header. The version is pinned at RAYLIB_VERSION, L92 — reading “6.5-dev” in a stable-looking library is your hint that master moves fast.
  • rcore is the only mandatory module; optional ones are compiled in or out through switches like SUPPORT_MODULE_RSHAPES, L39 in config.h, which is why the binary can shrink to what you use.
  • The startup chain is short and readable: InitWindow, L591 calls InitPlatform, then rlglInit, then loads the default font — three pages of C, not a framework bootstrap.
  • There is no class hierarchy; all shared state is one global struct, CoreData CORE, L405, which backends and modules both read and write.
  • Window and event code does not live in rcore.c at all: it lives in per-platform files like PollInputEvents, L1311, so the core calls a contract instead of an OS.
  • rlgl defaults to OpenGL 3.3 when no graphics API is defined — see GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_33, L158 — with explicit escape hatches for GL 1.1, 2.1, ES2 and ES3.
  • Shapes and text deliberately share one texture atlas: SetShapesTexture, L93 hands shapes the font’s white rectangle, so rectangles, circles and glyphs can ride a single batch.
  • Text is not a special path: DrawTextCodepoint, L1302 ends up in DrawTexturePro, exactly like a sprite does.
  • Audio is fully decoupled from the GL side — raudio.c is built on the bundled miniaudio.h, L177 include and would keep playing even if rendering died.

The detail view: follow InitWindow down into InitPlatform and rlglInit, then trace one frame from BeginDrawing through rlVertex3f's CPU buffers to the flush inside EndDrawing.

The Layer Cake: Five Modules and a Header

raylib’s source tree is organized the way its log messages describe it. When InitWindow, L617 starts up it prints the module list — rcore and rlgl marked mandatory, rshapes, rtextures, rtext, rmodels and raudio marked optional. That is not marketing; each module is one compilation unit (or one header) and each can be switched off in config.h before building. The layering is strictly downward: rshapes pushes vertices, rtextures uploads and samples textures, rtext calls rtextures, rmodels drives shaders, and all of them land on rlgl, which alone talks to raw OpenGL. Nothing above rcore knows that a GPU exists.

Inside rcore.c the sections are literal — comments divide Window and Graphics Device (from L544), Screen Drawing (from L857), and Timing (from L1574). If you have ever wanted to know “where would frame pacing live,” the file layout answers before grep does.

rcore: A Frame Is a Timestamp, a Matrix, and a Swap

Look at what the bracket actually does. BeginDrawing, L868 stamps the current time to measure your update phase, resets the modelview matrix with rlLoadIdentity, and applies the screen-scale matrix — that is all. It is cheap on purpose so you can call it once per frame without guilt. Even ClearBackground, L861 is just two rlgl calls to set the clear color and flush the framebuffer bits.

EndDrawing, L885 is where everything deferred gets paid for, in order: first rlDrawRenderBatchActive, L887 uploads and draws whatever vertices your game queued; then SwapScreenBuffer flips the back buffer; then a small timing block computes draw time against the target frame time and calls WaitTime to sleep off the remainder — the frame-pacing system at L896 is the reason a naive raylib loop holds 60 FPS without any of your code. Finally PollInputEvents runs so keyboard and mouse state are fresh for the next frame’s update, and if you pressed F12 a screenshot is written. Camera transitions fit the same pattern: BeginMode2D, L930 must flush the batch before swapping the modelview matrix, because the queued vertices were recorded with the old transform.

rlgl: Immediate Mode, Emulated

The deepest trick in raylib is that rlgl looks like old-school immediate mode but behaves like a modern batched renderer. The whole engine is a header — version stamped RLGL_VERSION, L113 — holding one static state struct, rlglData RLGL, L1118. Startup, rlglInit, L2258, creates the boring-but-critical assets: a 1x1 white texture for untextured shapes, the default shader pair, the default render batch, and a matrix stack explicitly built to emulate OpenGL 1.1.

When rshapes “draws” a rectangle it opens a primitive with rlBegin, L1452 and calls rlVertex2f per corner — but nothing reaches the driver yet. Each vertex is CPU-transformed by the current modelview and appended to plain C arrays inside the batch: rlVertex3f, L1495 writes position, texcoord, normal and color into a preallocated buffer. When that buffer fills, an overflow check hands control to rlCheckRenderBatchLimit, L3205, which drains the batch and quietly starts a new one. rlDrawRenderBatchActive, L3196 is the flush used both by EndDrawing and by any mid-frame texture change, which is how rlSetTexture, L1638 keeps one draw call per texture run instead of per sprite. If you have read how Alacritty batches its glyph grid, this is the same idea — amortize the driver with big vertex streams — arrived at from the opposite direction.

The 3D modules do not ride the quad batch; they bind real programs. DrawMesh, L1491 calls rlEnableShader with the material’s shader id and issues vertex-array draws directly, which is why shaders feel first-class in raylib’s 3D path.

One Contract, Ten Platform Files

The reason rcore.c compiles everywhere is that it never touches a windowing API. InitWindow delegates to InitPlatform, and each file in src/platforms/ implements that contract for one target: GLFW, SDL, RGFW and Win32 for desktop, DRM/KMS for card-slot Linux, Android, two web variants, and even a memory-only framebuffer with no OS. The GLFW backend is the default: InitPlatform runs glfwInit, glfwCreateWindow, L1690 makes the window, and the contract’s swap function is a one-liner — SwapScreenBuffer, L1212 — wrapping glfwSwapBuffers. Time comes from glfwGetTime, L1222, input lands in CORE.Input, and rcore.c neither knows nor cares. The same contract is what lets the web backend feed a browser canvas and the DRM backend drive a framebuffer with no display server at all.

From CMake Build to First Window

The library builds with either toolchain from the src/ directory. With make, the platform is a variable — PLATFORM ?= PLATFORM_DESKTOP, L70 maps to PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW unless you override it with, say, PLATFORM_DESKTOP_SDL or PLATFORM_DRM — and the library type defaults to static via RAYLIB_LIBTYPE ?= STATIC, L89, so make PLATFORM=PLATFORM_DESKTOP RAYLIB_LIBTYPE=SHARED gets you a shared object. With CMake, src/CMakeLists.txt declares the project at PROJECT_VERSION 6.2.0, L3. One honest note for source readers: the Makefile still says 6.2.0 while raylib.h on master reports 6.5-dev — release strings lag the dev branch.

A first window is then deliberately boring: InitWindow(800, 450, "hi"); while (!WindowShouldClose()) { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); DrawText("frame one", 20, 20, 20, DARKBLUE); EndDrawing(); } — five calls, no callbacks, no objects. The equivalent loop in Bevy gives you an ECS scheduler instead; raylib gives you a while-loop and expects nothing else.

Honest Limits

raylib trades ambition for legibility, and the limits are visible in the tree, not hidden behind documentation. There is no scene graph, no editor, no asset browser, and no animation graph — raylib.h offers types and functions, and the structure of your game is your problem. The rendering backend covers OpenGL variants only (the API switches at rlgl.h, L25 list GL 1.1 through ES3); there is no Vulkan, Metal or DirectX path, so on modern Apple hardware you are living inside MoltenGL-style translation rather than native Metal. The 3D path is honest about its age too: on the GL 1.1 backend DrawMesh, L1452 falls back to client-side state pointers, and 3D meshes are not merged into the 2D-style batch. External dependencies are bundled wholesale in src/external/ — miniaudio, the stb family, glad, cgltf, tinyobj — which is what makes single-file builds possible, at the cost of vendored code that will not update itself. None of this is accidental: config.h, L39 lets you compile the library down to exactly the modules you use. If those trade-offs match your project — a tool, a jam game, a teaching demo, or the rendering core of a Zig side project — the ceiling is low but the floor is remarkably high.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of raylib: how rcore, rlgl, and the platform backends cooperate to turn BeginDrawing/EndDrawing into real OpenGL draw calls.

entry.title: Inside SDL3: How the Cross-Platform Media Layer Absorbs Every OS

link.title: Inside SDL3: How the Cross-Platform Media Layer Absorbs Every OS

entry.content:
Ask anyone who has shipped a native app on three operating systems: the windowing layer is where optimism goes to die. On Windows you fight message loops and DPI, on macOS you fight the main thread and lifecycle events, on Linux you fight Wayland versus X11 before you have drawn a single pixel. Full engines such as Godot carry dedicated platform-abstraction teams just for this layer, and most small studios end up hand-rolling a worse version. Simple DirectMedia Layer has been the shared answer since the 1990s, and the SDL3 rewrite is the most interesting version of it: one small C library that promises window, input, audio, and rendering on two dozen platforms from a single API.

Open the source tree and the first surprise is how the trick works. Your SDL_PollEvent call never talks to the operating system. It reads from a private, mutex-guarded linked list of events that platform threads keep filling up behind your back. Everything OS-specific lives behind compile-time driver tables, so on Linux the video bootstrap contains Wayland and X11 side by side, and your code never learns which one won.

The second surprise is that SDL3 now ships two drawing systems side by side: the classic SDL_Renderer for portable 2D, and the brand-new SDL_GPU API, an explicit, shader-based abstraction over Vulkan, Direct3D 12, and Metal. Understanding when each one loads, and what code runs under each, is the key to reading this codebase. This post walks through both, plus the event queue and the redesigned audio stack, using the actual sources.

SDL3 at a glance: one init path fans out into compile-time platform drivers (video), one global event queue, two drawing stacks (SDL_Renderer over SDL_GPU and friends), and the audio subsystem. Every arrow is a real call direction in the tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SDL_internal.h, L63 — every translation unit starts from this one umbrella header, which pulls in the generated build config and the dynamic API shims, so feature flags are decided exactly once per build.
  • SDL_InitSubSystem, L341 — subsystems are refcounted here; asking for video quietly brings up events, keyboard, mouse, touch, and pen.
  • bootstrap, L82 — the video driver table is a plain compile-time array; on Linux both Wayland and X11 sit in it, with Wayland marked preferred next to X11 at Wayland_preferred_bootstrap, L91.
  • SDL_InitVideo, L622 — driver selection honors the SDL_HINT_VIDEO_DRIVER hint first, then walks the table calling each driver’s create function from the loop at L679.
  • SDL_EventQ, L152 — one global queue: a mutex, an atomic count, a live list, and a free list of SDL_EventEntry, L144 nodes that get recycled.
  • SDL_PollEvent, L1602 — literally SDL_WaitEventTimeoutNS with a zero timeout; the waiting logic with joystick pumping and the poll sentinel lives in SDL_WaitEventTimeoutNS, L1732.
  • render_drivers, L109 — SDL_Renderer is itself a driver table: D3D11, D3D12, Metal, OpenGL, GLES2, PS2, PSP, and others, including a modern entry implemented on top of SDL_GPU in src/render/gpu/SDL_render_gpu.c.
  • backends, L319 — SDL_GPU ships exactly three real backends, Metal, D3D12, and Vulkan, chosen at device-creation time.
  • SDL_OpenAudioDeviceStream, L2352 — audio is expressed as streams bound to logical devices; format conversion, buffering, and mixing live in SDL_audiocvt.c, SDL_audioqueue.c, and SDL_mixer.c.

The detail view: platform drivers on the left post into the event queue, init reaches every subsystem, the renderer and GPU stacks select concrete backends, and Linux core glue feeds device hotplug to both video and audio.

One Entry Point, Many Drivers

Every SDL3 program starts the same way: SDL_Init or SDL_InitSubSystem bumps a refcount and initializes what that subsystem depends on. Request SDL_INIT_VIDEO and SDL_InitVideo first spins up events, keyboard, mouse, touch, and pen, then picks a platform driver. The candidate list is the bootstrap array cited above — from Windows, Cocoa, UIKit, Android, and Emscripten to console ports like PS2, PSP, and Vita — and each entry is a tiny struct with a name and a create function pointer. If you pass a driver name via hint, SDL tries each comma-separated candidate; otherwise it walks the table in order and takes the first driver whose create succeeds.

What makes this scale is that SDL never calls the platform again by name. After selection, the library holds a SDL_VideoDevice whose function pointers do everything: pump events, create and destroy windows, manage displays, GL and Vulkan contexts. Window creation shows the modern pattern — the simple SDL_CreateWindow, L2642 just packs its arguments into properties and forwards to SDL_CreateWindowWithProperties, L2416, so one extensible entry point serves every platform without signature churn. The Linux core glue in src/core/linux (udev device scanning, D-Bus for screensaver inhibition) is shared by whatever video and audio drivers got picked, which is why the diagram wires core as its own group rather than part of video.

The Event Queue: How SDL_PollEvent Really Works

The event subsystem is small enough to read in one sitting, and it explains most of SDL’s personality. Platform side, each video driver implements PumpEvents — for Wayland that is the wl_seat dispatch loop in src/video/wayland/SDL_waylandevents.c, for X11 it is the XEvent translation in src/video/x11/SDL_x11events.c. Library side, SDL_PumpEvents, L1595 invokes the driver’s pump through _this->PumpEvents, L1575 and then runs maintenance: updating timestamps, flushing watches.

The queue itself is a doubly-linked list protected by one mutex. Events are pushed either by the driver or by any of your threads via SDL_PushEvent, L1858, which is just SDL_PeepEvents in add mode; the peep function at SDL_PeepEvents, L1270 is the single choke point for add, get, and peek with a type range filter. One clever detail: SDL_WaitEventTimeoutNS pushes a SDL_EVENT_POLL_SENTINEL marker into the queue, so when the drain loop sees the sentinel it knows it caught up and can block on the driver’s wait until the OS wakes something — that is how SDL gives you blocking waits without missing events that arrive mid-drain.

Three consequences for app authors. First, event memory belongs to SDL: the migration guide is explicit that you must copy strings out of drop and text events, since the nodes are recycled. Second, SDL2’s SDL_WINDOWEVENT wrapper is gone — window state changes arrive as top-level events, which the migration notes, L381 describe. Third, watchers registered with SDL_AddEventWatch see events as they are pushed, before any poll.

Two Ways to Draw: SDL_Renderer and SDL_GPU

SDL_Renderer remains the friendly 2D API: create one from a window with SDL_CreateRenderer, L1453, then draw textures and geometry without thinking about shaders. Underneath it is the same driver-table pattern as video — each backend implements texture upload, batching, and present. The backends span old and new: OpenGL and GLES2 for compatibility, D3D11, D3D12, Metal, even PS2 and PSP, plus a pure software rasterizer in src/render/software as the floor. If you know raylib, which solves the same “immediate 2D on a window” problem, SDL_Renderer is the part of SDL that plays that role — including the option to back it entirely by SDL_GPU through the driver in src/render/gpu/SDL_render_gpu.c.

SDL_GPU is the other end of the spectrum: an explicit, render-graph-free API in the Vulkan/D3D12 idiom — command buffers you fill and submit, explicit texture transfer, explicit state objects, swapchains you acquire per frame. The constraint is honest and visible in backends, L319: only Vulkan, D3D12, and Metal are implemented, because those are the APIs worth abstracting in 2026. Selection mirrors video: SDL_GPUSelectBackend, L604 refuses to run unless the video subsystem is already up, honors SDL_HINT_GPU_DRIVER, then asks each backend’s PrepareDriver whether the hardware qualifies before SDL_CreateGPUDevice, L707 instantiates it. Shader inputs are declared per device as SPIR-V, DXBC, DXIL, MSL, or metallib, so you compile offline per target.

A frame looks like: acquire a swapchain texture (SDL_AcquireGPUSwapchainTexture, L3354), record passes into a command buffer, then hand it over with SDL_SubmitGPUCommandBuffer, L3445. Apps like Alacritty that render text with OpenGL cross-platform had to solve this window-plus-GPU plumbing themselves on top of winit; SDL3 packages the same machinery for C.

Audio Without Callbacks: Devices, Streams, Mixers

SDL3’s audio redesign leans on a small number of verbs. Enumerate hardware with SDL_GetAudioPlaybackDevices, L1571 — physical devices, the real outputs your OS knows about. Opening one with SDL_OpenAudioDevice, L2004 yields a logical device; bind one or more SDL_AudioStreams to it, and SDL_OpenAudioDeviceStream, L2352 is the one-call shortcut that does both. The stream is where SDL3’s value lives: it accepts whatever format, sample rate, and channel count your data is in, and the conversion machinery in SDL_audiocvt.c (backed by the ring buffers of SDL_audioqueue.c) reshapes it to the device’s format. For mixing into the final output there is SDL_mixer.c, and for last-word DSP you can attach a callback with SDL_SetAudioPostmixCallback, L2135, which runs over the device thread’s mixed float buffer.

The old callback-centric API is gone on purpose: SDL2’s SDL_LockAudioDevice/SDL_UnlockAudioDevice pair was removed because there is no user callback thread left to protect — streams maintain their own locks and are documented as safe from any thread. That also means SDL3 will not implicitly initialize the audio subsystem when you open a device; you must call SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_AUDIO) yourself. Backend coverage matches the video story: WASAPI on Windows, coreaudio on Apple, and pulseaudio, ALSA, JACK, and PipeWire among the options on Linux, with hotplug events when udev or the OS reports changes.

From CMake Build to First Window

The documented build is three commands. On Windows, per the README, L24: cmake -S . -B build, then cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo, then cmake --install build --config RelWithDebInfo --prefix C:/SDL. On UNIX the same flow installs to /usr/local with sudo cmake --install build --prefix /usr/local. Useful switches: -DSDL_TESTS=ON builds the test programs, -DSDL_EXAMPLES=ON the examples, and -DSDL_SHARED/-DSDL_STATIC pick library flavors. The repo even ships a 67-line hello.c demonstrating the callback style.

Then a game links it via find_package(SDL3 REQUIRED CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS SDL3-shared) and target_link_libraries(mygame PRIVATE SDL3::SDL3), or vendors the source with add_subdirectory. In hello.c, SDL_MAIN_USE_CALLBACKS replaces main with SDL_AppInit, SDL_AppEvent, and SDL_AppIterate; init calls SDL_CreateWindowAndRenderer("Hello World", 800, 600, SDL_WINDOW_FULLSCREEN, ...) — note the title moved into the first parameter in SDL3 — and the event callback returns SDL_APP_SUCCESS on SDL_EVENT_QUIT or a keydown, ending the app without you managing a loop at all. For comparison, Rust projects like Bevy consume the same platform services through their own windowing layer; SDL3 keeps that whole layer in one C library you can vendor and forget.

Honest Limits

SDL3 is a breaking rewrite, and the migration guide is the honest map. SDL_RenderCopy became SDL_RenderTexture and returns bool (migration, L1412); SDL_CreateWindow no longer takes a position; fullscreen is now an explicit mode set with SDL_SetWindowFullscreenMode, and SDL_WINDOW_FULLSCREEN_DESKTOP is gone. The SDLmain library was replaced by the header-only SDL_main.h. Event memory is owned by SDL. Each of these will break an SDL2 codebase that compiles cleanly, and the dynamic API does not paper over them.

SDL_GPU’s scope is a genuine limitation, not a bug: three backends means Vulkan-class, D3D12-class, or Metal-class hardware only. There is deliberately no OpenGL implementation, so old GPUs and some emulated environments fall back to SDL_Renderer or software. Backend selection also depends on video being initialized first — calling SDL_GPU before SDL_INIT_VIDEO fails by design. Finally, the CMake FAQ notes that on Linux the build requires X11 or Wayland development packages unless you explicitly opt out, and per-driver feature coverage still varies; the README-wayland and README-linux docs list the caveats per platform. SDL3 absorbs the differences, but reading the per-platform docs before shipping remains part of the job.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of SDL3: the video bootstrap table, the event queue, SDL_GPU vs SDL_Renderer, audio streams, and how platform backends hide every OS behind one C API.

entry.title: Inside SFML: How the Module System Turns Vertices into Pixels

link.title: Inside SFML: How the Module System Turns Vertices into Pixels

entry.content:
If you have ever written a 2D game against raw SDL, you know the ritual: create a window, create a renderer, fill a rect, call SDL_RenderPresent, and only then start worrying about textures, blending, and scaling. SFML hides all of that behind a single line of code — window.draw(sprite) — and somehow it still feels fast. That combination of “one obvious call” and respectable performance is exactly why C++ developers keep picking it up. But when a call is that short, the interesting engineering is invisible, and invisible engineering is what this blog is about.

The answer to “what does draw() actually do” lives in a deliberate piece of C++ architecture: sf::RenderWindow inherits from sf::Window and from sf::RenderTarget at the same time. The Window half owns the operating-system window and the OpenGL context; the RenderTarget half owns the vertex path that feeds that context. Everything you draw goes through one choke point — RenderTarget — and everything about how SFML feels is decided inside that choke point: which GL state gets set, when it is cached, and how many function calls a sprite costs.

We cloned the master branch of SFML/SFML (version 3.x, C++17, built with CMake 3.28 or newer) and traced the full journey of a vertex: from sf::Sprite, through sf::RenderTarget, down to a raw glDrawArrays call. Along the way we found a rendered-out audio backend, a five-way platform split for GL contexts, and a state cache whose design notes are literally written into the source as a comment block. The two diagrams below map the whole system; every claim in this post links to the exact source line that backs it.

Overview of the five SFML modules and the spine that connects them: System feeds Window, Window feeds Graphics, and Audio and Network stand alongside as independent modules.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The System module is deliberately tiny: sf::Time is a header-only constexpr value type with seconds()/milliseconds() factories (Time.hpp, L41), and it is the currency the rest of the library pays its timing in.
  • sf::Window::create() pairs two platform objects: a WindowImpl for OS events and a GlContext for rendering (Window::create, L85). That pairing is the whole Window module in one line.
  • GlContext::create() funnels every platform through a shared-context manager that instantiates a ContextType — WGL, GLX, or EGL — and locks a mutex while doing it (GlContext::create, L576). GL entry points are loaded with glad (GlContext.cpp, L34).
  • sf::RenderWindow is the marriage of the two worlds: its constructor deliberately routes around the base-class constructor (“it contains virtual function calls”) and calls Window::create() directly (RenderWindow::RenderWindow, L40), then onCreate() initializes the render-target half (RenderTarget::initialize, L117).
  • Every drawable object implements one pure virtual method, draw(RenderTarget&, RenderStates) (Drawable.hpp, L66). That interface is the only contract between game code and the renderer.
  • A sprite is not an object on the GPU. It is four CPU-side vertices uploaded as a TriangleStrip, with its texture and transform stuffed into RenderStates (Sprite::draw, L117).
  • The choke point: RenderTarget::draw(const Drawable&) is two lines long — it just calls back into the object (RenderTarget::draw, L342) — while the vertex-array overload next door does the real GL work.
  • The chain ends at drawPrimitives(), which maps SFML’s six primitive types onto OpenGL modes and issues the single glDrawArrays call that puts pixels on screen (RenderTarget::drawPrimitives, L890).
  • Audio has its own spine: sf::SoundBuffer decodes a whole file into PCM and reattaches every live sf::Sound using it when the buffer changes (SoundBuffer::update, L267), and the playback engine underneath is vendored miniaudio, not OpenAL (Miniaudio.cpp, L32).

The overview shows the skeleton, but the skeleton is not where SFML earns its “fast” reputation. For that you need the detail view, where the platform backends, the FBO implementation, and the streaming audio classes all become visible.

The detailed view: per-platform GL contexts (WGL/GLX/EGL), the RenderTarget draw flow with its FBO path, the miniaudio playback stack, and the Network socket family.

Five Modules, One Library

SFML’s source tree under src/SFML contains exactly six directories: System, Window, Graphics, Audio, Network, and a small Main helper for Android entry points. The dependency direction is strictly downward — Graphics calls into Window and System, Audio and Network call into System, and nothing calls up. This is what makes the CMake options in the root CMakeLists.txt honest: SFML_BUILD_WINDOW, SFML_BUILD_GRAPHICS, SFML_BUILD_AUDIO, and SFML_BUILD_NETWORK are independent toggles (CMakeLists.txt, L49), so you can link just sfml-window if you only need input and a context, which is precisely the setup many raylib and raw-GL projects use SFML for.

The split between sf::WindowBase and sf::Window is subtler and easy to miss. WindowBase owns everything that does not need OpenGL: the OS window handle, the event pump, and the pollEvent() loop, which since SFML 3 returns a std::optional<Event> (WindowBase::pollEvent, L142). Only sf::Window adds the GlContext. If you have ever embedded a rendering context into a GUI toolkit or a terminal emulator like Alacritty, you know why this boundary matters: window management and GL context ownership are two different fights, and SFML refuses to conflate them. An engine like Godot solves the same problem with a platform-abstraction layer hundreds of classes wide; SFML solves it with inheritance and two classes.

What draw() Actually Does

Call window.draw(sprite) and this is the exact chain. First, RenderTarget::draw(const Drawable&, const RenderStates&) performs virtual dispatch into the object, which multiplies its own transform into the states and hands back raw vertices (RenderTarget::draw, L342). The Transformable base class keeps position, rotation, scale, and origin as scalars and recombines them into a 3x3 matrix only when somebody asks — and caches the result until a setter dirties it (Transformable::getTransform, L122). So a static sprite costs zero matrix math per frame; a moving one costs one 3x3 multiply.

Then the vertex-array overload of draw() takes over (RenderTarget::draw, L349). If the batch is small enough, SFML pre-transforms the vertices on the CPU into an internal cache and later issues the draw with an identity modelview matrix (RenderTarget::draw, L358) — a neat trade of GPU matrix work for CPU pointer writes. setupDraw() then reconciles the desired state with what the GL state machine already holds: view, blend mode, stencil mode, texture, and shader are each rebound only if they changed since the last call (RenderTarget::setupDraw, L818). A long comment block at the bottom of the file explains each of these caching strategies, including why textures are tracked by a custom ID rather than a raw GL name — because GL IDs can be recycled after deletion (RenderTarget.cpp, L925).

Finally, the fixed-function GL calls land: glVertexPointer, glColorPointer, and optionally glTexCoordPointer describe the interleaved sf::Vertex layout (RenderTarget::draw, L394), and drawPrimitives() translates the primitive type enum and fires glDrawArrays (RenderTarget::drawPrimitives, L890). Every GL call is wrapped in glCheck, which logs errors in release builds and can be made fatal with a CMake flag. sf::RenderTexture reuses this exact machinery with a different backend: an FBO implementation that binds and unbinds framebuffer objects instead of the window surface, sharing all of the state-cache code.

From CMake Build to First Window

Building SFML from this tree is a two-command affair. The project requires CMake 3.28 as its floor (CMakeLists.txt, L1) and compiles as C++17 via target_compile_features(SFML PUBLIC cxx_std_17) (CMakeLists.txt, L281). Configure with -DSFML_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON if you want the sample programs (CMakeLists.txt, L394), or use -DSFML_USE_SYSTEM_DEPS=ON to link system freetype/vorbis/flac instead of the bundled ones (CMakeLists.txt, L112). The README recommends the official CMake project template, which downloads and builds SFML alongside your application (readme.md, L14) — a FetchContent flow that sidesteps manual installation entirely.

Now trace what happens between sf::RenderWindow window({800, 600}, "Title"); and the first frame. The constructor calls Window::create(), which first closes any existing window, then creates the platform WindowImpl (Window::create, L85) and the GlContext with your requested ContextSettings — depth bits, stencil bits, anti-aliasing level, version flags. Inside GlContext::create(), a process-wide shared context is created once and mutex-guarded; the new context is then instantiated as the platform ContextType and initialized against the requested settings (GlContext::create, L576). Back in RenderWindow, onCreate() records which framebuffer binding counts as the window’s default (important when FBOs are available) and runs RenderTarget::initialize(), which sets up default views and generates the unique ID that the state-tracking map uses to know whether this target is already active in the current context (RenderTarget::setActive, L483).

The event loop is the third piece. while (window.pollEvent(event)) pulls platform messages out of the WindowImpl queue through the std::optional-returning API, and window.display() flips the backbuffer by calling into the context (Window::display, L196). If you set a framerate limit, display() also sleeps out the difference between the frame time and the limit using the System module’s clock (Window::setFramerateLimit, L168). That is the entire runtime contract: pump events, draw, display.

Audio Without OpenAL

The most surprising thing in the Audio module is what is not there: OpenAL. Through SFML 2.x the audio stack was famously built on OpenAL, but SFML 3 removed the shared-library requirement entirely (the changelog records “Removed OpenAL shared library requirement” as a 3.0 change (changelog.md, L247)). The replacement is miniaudio, a single-file C library that SFML vendors and compiles directly into itself — the file literally contains #include <miniaudio.c> (Miniaudio.cpp, L32). For a game developer this means one less runtime DLL to ship and no more “OpenAL32.dll not found” support threads.

The data flow is classic resource/handle separation. sf::SoundBuffer owns decoded PCM samples for short sounds: its constructor throws sf::Exception if the file fails to load (SoundBuffer::SoundBuffer, L44), loading goes through sf::InputSoundFile, which dispatches to per-format readers for WAV, OGG/Vorbis, FLAC, and MP3 (SoundBuffer::loadFromFile, L108). The clever part is buffer mutation while playing: update() detaches every sf::Sound currently using the buffer, recomputes the duration, and reattaches them (SoundBuffer::update, L267) — the destructor does the same swap-then-detach dance to avoid iterator invalidation (SoundBuffer::~SoundBuffer, L93). Long audio takes the other path: sf::Music is a sf::SoundStream, which decodes the file in chunks on a background thread and never holds the whole PCM in memory. sf::Sound::play() just forwards the state change down to the miniaudio-backed implementation (Sound::play, L218).

Sockets, Packets, and Blocking Modes

The Network module is the smallest, and its design is the most conservative: thin RAII wrappers over BSD-sockets with a portable SocketSelector on top. sf::TcpSocket::connect() takes an IP address, port, and a sf::Time timeout, and returns a status enum rather than throwing (TcpSocket::connect, L840). Raw sends and receives return the number of bytes actually transferred so partial writes can be handled (TcpSocket::send, L1079). On top of the raw byte layer sits sf::Packet, which adds length-prefixed framing and stream operators so a send(packet) call transmits your typed payload as one message (TcpSocket::sendPacket, L1264). sf::TcpListener::accept() hands out connected sockets, sf::UdpSocket handles datagrams, and the selector multiplexes them all — enough to build a small authoritative server without pulling in a networking dependency.

Honest Limits

Reading the source also makes SFML’s boundaries clear, and the repository is refreshingly upfront about them. First, the rendering path is not a modern core-profile renderer: the code drives compatibility-style GL calls — client-side vertex arrays with glVertexPointer/glColorPointer, glMatrixMode/glLoadMatrixf for the projection — rather than shaders-and-VBOs everywhere (RenderTarget.cpp, L394). It is fast for 2D, but if you want GPU-resident batches the escape hatch is sf::VertexBuffer, and anything fancier means writing your own GL code against the context SFML hands you.

Second, version 3 is a real break with 2.x, and the migration guide spells it out: sf::Event is now a variant polled through std::optional, enumerations are scoped, sf::Angle replaces bare float degrees, and the C++ standard floor moved (migration.md, L169). The README states plainly that development is focused on version 3 in master and that no more features are planned for 2.x (readme.md, L9) — so codegen targets and tutorials aimed at 2.x will fight you. Third, scope: this is a 2D library; there is no scene graph, no 3D math, no asset tooling — the README describes the modules as windowing, graphics, audio, and network, nothing more. And fourth, the license: the code is zlib/libpng, free for commercial use with no attribution required, but the project ships it strictly “as-is, without any express or implied warranty” — the same disclaimer header sits at the top of every source file you just read.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of SFML's five modules - Window, Graphics, System, Audio and Network - and how window.draw() becomes an OpenGL draw call.
